title: BMW F 450 GS Prices Hiked By Up To Rs 30,000 - DriveSpark
content: BMW Motorrad India has increased prices across the F 450 GS range by up to Rs 30,000. The hike applies to all three variants, Base, Exclusive and GS Trophy, months after the motorcycle's introductory launch pricing. The Base and Exclusive variants have each gone up by Rs 25,000, while the range-topping GS Trophy has increased by Rs 30,000. BMW had stated at launch that the initial prices were introductory, hinting at a future revision. BMW introduced the F 450 GS earlier this year as its new entry-level ADV, replacing the long-discontinued G 310 GS in the country. The BMW F 450 GS stood out at launch for its Easy Ride Clutch (ERC), which removes the need to operate the clutch lever while shifting gears. All three variants of the F 450 GS have received a price increase: All prices are ex-showroom, Delhi. The BMW F 450 GS Exclusive variant gets an up-and-down quickshifter over the Base, while the GS Trophy adds the ERC and an adjustable USD fork on top of that. A Sport variant that would sit between the Exclusive and Trophy, with only the adjustable suspension, has not been brought to India. BMW has made no mechanical or feature changes alongside the price hike. The BMW F 450 GS continues with its 420cc, twin-cylinder, liquid-cooled engine that produces 48hp and 43Nm of torque. The ERC remains exclusive to the Trophy variant of the BMW F 450 GS , and heated grips continue as standard across the range. Cruise control is still missing, even as an optional accessory. Colour choices also stay unchanged. The Base and Exclusive variants are offered only in Cosmic Black, while the BMW F 450 GS GS Trophy gets a Racing Blue shade with red and white accents. title: Rivals Turned Teammates Silva, Suksom Target Championship - 조선일보
content: Former opponents join forces as GS Caltex aims to defend V-League title In last April’s women’s professional volleyball championship finals, Gisele Silva, 35 years old, Cuba, and Tanacha Suksom, 26 years old, Thailand, faced each other across the net. At the time, GS Caltex, led by Silva who averaged 34.7 points per game, defeated Tanacha Suksom’s Korea Expressway Corporation with a three-game sweep and claimed the top spot. Five months later, the two players now stand on the same court wearing the same uniform. This is because Tanacha Suksom, a former Thai national team member, joined GS Caltex as an Asian quota player for this season. On the 13th, the two, who met in Hitachinaka, Japan, where GS Caltex is holding its training camp, eagerly embraced each other as soon as photo shooting began, showcasing their unique “chemistry.” Tanacha Suksom said, “My three seasons at Korea Expressway Corporation were good memories, but I thought a new challenge was necessary to grow further,” and added, “At a time when I was considering a change, GS Caltex contacted me first, which led me to decide on the transfer.” The player who welcomed Tanacha Suksom’s joining the most was Silva. Silva said, “When I heard the news that I would be playing with Tanacha Suksom, who is good at defense and has fierce attacks, I thought we could show fans really exciting volleyball.” Silva will wear the GS Caltex uniform again in the 2026-2027 season, which opens on October 31, becoming the first foreign player in the V-League to play for the same team for four consecutive seasons. Last season, she recorded the regular league’s highest points (1,083 points) and highest attack success rate (47.33%), and in the postseason, she led the team to a six-game undefeated championship with six consecutive 30+ point games, sweeping both the regular league and championship finals MVP awards. Breaking 1,000 points for three consecutive seasons is also a record Silva first set in the V-League. For Silva, “1,000 points” is a great source of pride, but from the team’s perspective, it’s not entirely a positive record. This is because it means GS Caltex’s offense heavily relied on Silva. For GS Caltex to challenge for a second consecutive championship this season, Tanacha Suksom’s support will be crucial. Tanacha Suksom said, “To achieve another championship, each player must take responsibility and fulfill their role.” Although the two had stared each other down and engaged in a tense battle of nerves during the last championship finals, they have now become close friends who constantly exchange stories in English. Tanacha Suksom said, “I respect Jiji (Silva’s nickname), who excellently fulfills both roles as a mother and a professional athlete.” Silva said, “Experiencing last season’s championship win boosted all the players’ confidence,” and added, “With Tanacha Suksom joining, we will join forces with our great teammates to stand atop the summit again this season.”

title: "A GS with an LS:" Classic 1970 Buick Skylark Won't Make You Feel Blue About Its Few Modern Touches - autoevolution.com
content:
The Buick Skylark nameplate was made across six generations over the span of almost half a century, from 1953 through 1998, and remains an example of how the automotive realm has been dramatically reshaped over the years via advancing technology, changing buyer taste, and new standards. The A-body third generation was offered as a four-door hardtop or sedan and station wagon, as well as a two-door coupe, convertible, and hardtop. It was noted for its muscle car/personal luxury car appeal, and it shared components with the likes of the Acadian Beaumont, Buick Special, Chevrolet Chevelle, Pontiac Tempest and LeMans plus GTO, Oldsmobile F-85, Cutlass and Cutlass Supreme, or the Hurst/Olds and Buick GSX and Chevelle SS for the performance models. This 1970 Buick Skylark GS “is a striking example of classic Buick muscle reimagined with modern performance and drivability,” according to the dealership’s description. It went through a frame-off restoration combined with a few sensible modifications, and now this Skylark “combines the aggressive proportions and unmistakable styling of a first-generation GS with a thoroughly modernized mechanical package.” Outside, it’s dressed in a serene combination of Stratomist Blue and chrome trimmings, while inside there’s a classic black interior to show that despite the beautiful shade, nobody should feel blue about its classic car potential. There are also numerous chrome accents, larger Ridler aftermarket wheels, and a contemporary heart. That’s because under the hood resides a 5.3-liter LS V8 paired to a 4L60E automatic transmission, offering modern performance and reliability to the classic Buick. Plus, there’s power steering and air conditioning to “further enhance the driving experience, making this Skylark far more comfortable and usable than a typical vintage muscle car.” The chassis has also been updated to match the powertrain: it features a coilover suspension setup, front power disc brakes, and a few other modern touches. However, once you’re inside, the vintage atmosphere is still present and accounted for. The company says that you’ll have “a unique muscle car that grabs attention at the cruise-in while holding the road on the cruise out.” But how much does it cost? Well, the aftermarket dealership asks exactly $67,900, which is less than the starting price of a 2027 C8 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray, for example. Maybe that’s not a good comparison, but sadly that’s the only remaining passenger car line sold by General Motors in the mainstream sector, along with Cadillac’s outgoing CT4 and the surviving CT5 luxury sedans. So, what do you think – would you buy this 1970 Buick Skylark GS featuring an LS or not? title: Kim Ji-won Seeks Redemption, Second Title with Tana Char - 조선일보
content: GS Caltex setter targets consecutive championships after regrets from limited spring play [Sports Chosun Kim Young-rok Reporter] "I’ve won two championships, but I still have some regrets about not being able to play many games in the spring volleyball season. I want to show a different side this year." The joy of the championship setter was short-lived, as the women’s volleyball offseason is brief. GS Caltex’s Kim Ji-won is burning with determination to win the new season. GS Caltex continues its fourth year alongside the 'Cuban monster' Giselle Silva. However, Silva, born in 1991, will turn 36 years old next year. She herself has said, "This is the twilight of my playing career. I want to retire while I can still show my skills to the fans." Naturally, GS Caltex’s focus is on the present rather than the future. The core player who must lead the team 'now' is Kim Ji-won. Regarding her post-championship vacation, Kim Ji-won said, "There was nothing special. However, I was surprised to find I had gained weight after taking a long break from exercise. Now, my body feels lighter again," and laughed. She is gradually returning to practice matches in preparation for the season opener. "In my first year, our team achieved a treble (winning the cup tournament, regular season, and championship finals all in a single season). I couldn’t do anything due to injuries that season. Last season was different. Since I directly contributed to the matches, even after winning the championship, I couldn’t believe it. I don’t know how many times I rewatched the championship match footage during the offseason." It was a season where her skills truly flourished. She played 35 games and 109 sets, exceeding 1,200 sets with a 1200-set accuracy. Her average of 11.03 sets per game is her best record since her debut. Kim Ji-won reflected, "Since the team’s performance wasn’t great, I struggled mentally during preparation. As the season progressed, our momentum improved, and the good results made me very happy." Previously, GS Caltex, which had failed to advance to the spring volleyball season despite two seasons with league-best foreign player Silva, barely made it to the spring volleyball after a fierce battle until the final game of last season, Silva’s third year in Korea. Once there, everything changed. They dominated the court with a perfect 6-0 record against Jungwon Life Insurance, Hyundai Engineering & Construction, and Korea Expressway Corporation, clinching their first championship in five years. However, there was a slight regret in the process. The regular season was operated primarily around Kim Ji-won, but as the season ended, the role of An Hye-jin (free agent), who returned from injury, grew larger. Ultimately, An Hye-jin was the starting setter in the spring volleyball. Kim Ji-won said, "It wasn’t just me who led the team to the spring volleyball," but added, "There’s still some regret. We won the championship, but I didn’t get to play much." She continued, "Still, if it’s the way the team can win, I think I was still lacking." The biggest wall in her career has been Hyundai Engineering & Construction. GS Caltex has struggled every year against Hyundai Engineering & Construction’s high blocks due to their weak middle blockers. Kim Ji-won sensed victory after winning the first playoff game against Hyundai Engineering & Construction. This season, she also named Hyundai Engineering & Construction as the most burdensome team. Although Yang Hyo-jin and Lee Da-hyun have left, the team remains formidable with Kim Da-in still present, joined by Bae Yu-na and Mega. Kim Ji-won was selected as the first overall pick in the rookie draft and joined GS Caltex. At the time, many volleyball insiders questioned the choice of Kim Ji-won over Lee Sun-woo (Jung Kwan Jang) and Choi Jung-min (Industrial Bank of Korea (IBK)). However, GS Caltex proved that their first picks, from Han Soo-jin to Kim Ji-won, were not surprises. Kim Ji-won laughed, "As a rookie, I felt pressured. It was unexpected, and there were so many negative comments. Now, I feel more at ease." GS Caltex’s clubhouse is located in the mountains of Cheongpyeong. Kim Ji-won said, "In summer, there are so many bugs that we can’t open the windows. In winter, when it snows a lot, cars slip on the uphill roads. That’s why I bought a four-wheel-drive car. During peak summer season, the roads get completely clogged," but added, "We have to drive to the convenience store. The facilities are amazing. It’s truly the best place to focus on training," and laughed. This year, GS Caltex strengthened its wing line by adding Tana Char as an Asian quota player, joining Silva. Tana Char’s transfer comes from the team they faced in last season’s championship finals. The chemistry between Kim Ji-won and Tana Char could be a key factor in this season’s performance. "When she was on the opposite side of the net, Silva and Tana Char felt similar—roaring and overwhelming. Now that we’re on the same team, I realized they’re more four-dimensional than I thought. It’s hard to explain. Even though Silva is my senior, she has a cute side. With Silva and Tana Char, my role will definitely expand. This year, I want to show more diverse aspects. I want to become a setter like Han Seon-su (Hanwha Aerospace) who maintains strong mental resilience and leads the team even in difficult situations."

title: Kim Ji-won vows diversify GS Caltex attack beyond Silva - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
content: "It was the first time I personally played and won a championship. So the emotions were extraordinary.". For GS Caltex women's professional volleyball setter Kim Ji-won (25), last season's championship is a memory she cannot easily forget. Even after reaching the top in the championship final, it didn't feel real for a while, so she replayed the game footage several times. Only then did she think, "we really won." But now it's time to move on from that sweet memory. Met at the Hitachinaka training camp in Ibaraki prefecture, Japan, on the 12th, Kim Ji-won said, "We can't remain drunk on the championship now. There is a consensus within the team that we need to move on quickly from last season's title." Now entering her seventh V League season, the weight on Kim Ji-won's shoulders has grown heavier. With Ahn Hye-jin's departure, her role and responsibilities in the setter rotation have increased. Having experienced both attacker and setter in high school, Kim Ji-won still says setter is a difficult position. She said, "If I had to pick the more physically demanding position it would be attacker, but the one that makes your head more complicated is definitely setter," adding, "truthfully, setter is not the position where I shine." Instead, there is a thrill that only a setter can feel when an attack that started from her fingertips is completed as a score. Kim Ji-won said, "With a good set that leaves only one blocker following or none at all, and the attacker scores, it's truly thrilling." There are tasks to solve ahead of the new season. One is building chemistry with Thanacha Suksod, who joined as the Asian quota player (Thailand). She is now so familiar with long-time teammate Giselle Silva that they know each other's preferred balls without many words. In contrast, Thanacha is a new type of attacker. Kim Ji-won confessed, "Her style is different from anything I've experienced before, so it's novel and still a bit difficult." That's why they increase conversations at every practice. It's a process of asking about the height and speed of the balls Thanacha prefers and aligning the tosses directly to find touch points. The Japanese training camp is also proving to be good study for Kim Ji-won. Facing fast and precise Japanese volleyball firsthand is broadening her vision as a setter. She said, "When you play Japanese teams it's so fast it's dizzying. But once you adapt to that speed, you feel you've grown," adding, "Japanese setters are so good there is much to learn." Advice from Japanese coach Ishii Suguru, who joined GS Caltex this season, is also a big help. Coach Ishii is in charge of setters. Kim Ji-won said, "He is usually a very funny person, but when training starts he becomes very serious," adding, "After yesterday's practice he called me over and I thought he would talk about toss control. But he said that because the opponent's play is fast, my play had become hurried as well. It was impressive that he looked at the whole match and gave advice." A new competitor has also emerged. On the 4th, GS Caltex acquired 177 cm tall setter Park Sa-rang from SOOP through a trade. Rather than be shaken by the competition, Kim Ji-won intends to focus on what she must do. She cited her steady temperament as one of her strengths. The goal is clear. She wants to be judged as having improved over last season, and above all to hear that "her play has become more varied." Over the past three seasons, GS Caltex has relied heavily on Silva in attack, with Silva scoring more than 1,000 points each season. Kim Ji-won's new task is to make use of Silva as a definite weapon while also distributing opportunities evenly to other attackers. "You can't only look at Silva," Kim Ji-won said, stressing, "I want to play volleyball that uses other attackers evenly so the opponent cannot easily predict us." The joy of first-time victory has now been left as a memory. Kim Ji-won's sights are not on the title of "championship setter" but on becoming a setter who has grown one level. title: Oh Se-yeon Targets Quick Attack Improvement for GS Caltex - 조선일보
content: Middle blocker aims to boost blocking and quick attacks after championship win Until middle school, volleyball was merely a sport I watched on TV. I fell in love with volleyball while watching the 2016 Rio Olympics and later pursued a player’s path during high school. Though my start was much later than my peers, I am now preparing for my seventh professional season. Last season, I also contributed significantly to GS Caltex’s championship finals victory. Oh Se-yeon, 24 years old, who was interviewed at the GS Caltex training camp in Hitachinaka, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan on the 12th, said, “Since I started volleyball late—a fact I cannot change—I try to compensate by working harder on my weaknesses.” Last season’s championship held special meaning for Oh Se-yeon. In her debut season, GS Caltex achieved a treble by winning the KOVO Cup, regular league, and championship finals, but she was mostly on the sidelines then. Oh Se-yeon remarked, “Winning by actually playing last season made it feel more valuable.” The most memorable match was the third game of the championship finals. She recorded eight blocks, lifting her team to the top. Oh Se-yeon smiled and said, “That day, the opponent’s attacks were strangely visible.” As a middle blocker, Oh Se-yeon is not particularly tall at 180 cm, but she compensates with her long arms and jumping ability. She explained, “Since my jumping is decent, I am confident in side blocking while moving. However, quick attack blocking requires jumping in place, which I still find challenging. It’s an area I need to improve.” Now in her seventh professional season, the biggest weapon Oh Se-yeon aims to reclaim this season is blocking. Compared to the 2024-2025 season—her first as a starter—she felt her blocking performance last season was unsatisfactory. She receives detailed guidance from head coach Lee Young-taek, a former middle blocker. Oh Se-yeon said, “When blocking, my hands tend to fall back, so the coach often advises me to push them forward more. I’m also practicing to time my quick attacks and maintain proper form even when my balance is disrupted.” She is equally eager to improve her quick attacks. Last season, GS Caltex heavily relied on Gisele Silva in attacks. If middle blockers actively engage in central attacks, they can distract opponents’ blockers and reduce pressure on Silva. Oh Se-yeon stated, “If I score more attack points, opponents will struggle to focus solely on Silva. This year, I want to increase my quick attacks.”

content: Subscribe to the HotCars newsletter to never miss an update You'll kick yourself for missing this undervalued Buick muscle car that terrorized Chevelle models at the drag strip. It’s an overlooked high-performance bargain you can scoop up for a fraction of the cost. It outsmarted rivals back in the day by dodging high insurance premiums, making it an excellent buy. Now it continues its legacy by outsmarting collectors, hiding in plain sight as buyers spend excessive amounts on more expensive models with similar power under different badges. Born in 1991, I missed the muscle car glory days, but I've spent time discussing sleeper options to make up for it. The point is that for decades people have described Buick as a brand for older buyers. The brand is also described as incredibly luxurious, with refined models appealing to an older demographic. In the 1960s, Buick wanted to shake its reputation as a luxury brand for older buyers by breaking into the booming muscle car market. To attract younger buyers instead of families, it decided to take a swing at rivals like the Pontiac GTO and Chevelle SS by launching a high-performance line. This effort involved keeping prices low to compete while producing enough raw power to challenge the competition. So, a massive big-block V8 engine was stuffed under the hood of a smaller, lightweight frame to gain authentic street credibility while maintaining upscale comfort that it already had a reputation for. Some will say the Buick’s swing missed and failed as the muscle car project didn’t last long. However, Buick is one of the prominent historic brands that still survives today, while Pontiac was retired long ago. But Buick still has the same reputation for building comfortable grocery haulers as its classic muscle car goes unnoticed. The Grand Sport has entered the conversation. The 1968-1969 Buick GS 400 is a serious contender with a 400 cubic-inch (6.5-liter) big-block V8 that’s factory-rated at 340 horsepower and 440 lb-ft of torque. It can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in about 6.5 seconds and complete a quarter mile in roughly 15.2 seconds at 92 mph with a top speed of around 130 mph. The 1968 Pontiac GTO 400 H.O. can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in around 6.4 seconds with a 14.2-second quarter-mile time at roughly 98 mph with a top speed of 126 mph. Then the Chevelle SS 396 accelerates from 0 to 60 mph in about 6.5 seconds and eats a quarter mile in around 14.4 seconds at 105 mph with a top speed of 130 mph. The Buick GS 400 rides on the redesigned A-Body platform with a 112-inch wheelbase and features an aggressive semi-fastback roofline paired with an S-shaped sweep spear sideline. The engine features a 4.04 x 3.90-inch bore and stroke, a 10.25:1 compression ratio, and hydraulic lifters. It breathes through a 750-CFM Rochester four-barrel carburetor, two-inch intake valves, and 1.62-inch exhaust valves with a dual exhaust. The Stage 1 package boosts power to 350 hp. It includes a camshaft upgrade, heavy-duty valve springs, a higher-pressure 60 PSI oil pump, and performance carburetion/transmission tuning. The 1968 Buick GS 400 had an original price of about $2,926 for the hardtop coupe, while the convertible started at around $3,271. Meanwhile, the 1968 Chevelle SS started at around $3,100, and the Pontiac GTO 400 H.O. started at $3,101. It was competitively priced and managed to avoid higher insurance premiums by having a conservative look that didn't draw attention. Its sophisticated style was part of the problem; the Chevelle SS and Pontiac GTO had much bolder styles with stripes, aggressive fender lines, and high-performance visual cues to attract younger buyers. Other muscle cars projected a stripped-down street performance attitude that was in high demand. Names like Chevelle and GTO were already more established as popular muscle car nameplates, while Buick carried an upscale, family-car reputation. Buick maintained a traditional advertising approach while Chevrolet and Pontiac actively marketed to younger buyers in the racing and pop culture scenes. The Buick GS 400 was famously “fast with class,” which appealed to those looking for more comfort instead of a stripped-down, brawling nature. It features deep-twist carpeting, wood-grain accents, plush bucket seats, an upscale instrument cluster with a tachometer, and other luxury appointments. But unfortunately, it faced much lower sales than its rivals. People passed on the Buick GS 400 in the late 1960s, and many still don't know what they're missing today. It’s more affordable than rivals despite being much rarer. In 1969, the Chevelle SS 396 sold roughly 90,000 units, while the GS 400 moved about 1,256 hardtop coupes and 212 convertibles equipped with the Stage 1 package. The value of the Buick GS 400 in average condition starts around $17,400. Models that have been well maintained typically sell for closer to $32,500. Convertible models in show quality will cross the auction block for up to $65,000. A few extremely high-profile examples have eclipsed the $80,000 mark. Meanwhile, the 1969 Chevy Chevelle SS 396 starts at about $20,000 for models in rough condition. Examples that are in good driving condition will sell for between $50,000 and $60,000. Then models in pristine condition fetch between $65,000 and over $100,000. Convertibles attract the highest premiums. The 1969 Pontiac GTO 400 H.O. Ram Air III fetches between $79,000 and $110,000, while the Ram Air IV hardtop models sell for between $150,000 and over $250,000. Judge and convertible options will fly past $600,000. The Buick GS 400 is well worth considering as an affordable way to enter the market, offering a unique style and plenty of power while saving thousands. We want to hear from you. title: This Citroen GS Concept Isn't Real, Unfortunately, and It Dwells Across Some Parallel CGI Universes - autoevolution.com
content:
Citroen introduced the iconic DS model in 1955, and it became an even more luxurious executive car compared to the innovative Traction Avant, so it had a sizeable gap in the model range between the cheap Ami and 2CV models and the luxurious DS around the 1970s. That need for a bridge among them was filled by the Citroen GS in 1970, and the car immediately won the European Car of the Year for 1971, mostly thanks to its DS-inspired and technologically advanced design, the class-leading comfort and safety, plus the aerodynamic body. It also had an instantly-recognizable four-door fastback silhouette which was carried on by its successors, the cheap ZX and the more upscale BX. The model was produced in places like Chile, Indonesia, Mozambique, Portugal and Spain, South Africa, Yugoslavia or Thailand, in addition to France, thus cementing a cult status place in global, not just European, automotive culture. So, are we surprised that folks continue to remember it, even some four decades after its retirement? More precisely, this time around we’re dealing with a member of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI - Mike G., the leader of the 'mike.g.concepts' design studio, "fueled by adrenaline and innovation," has reworked the classic Citroen GS/GSA into a modern EV, aiming to take advantage of Citroen’s legacy and of Stellantis’ propensity for all-electric powertrains. The author’s Citroen GS/GSA concept “transforms the original’s famous aerodynamic silhouette into an exercise in modern minimalism” as he uses “crisp” LED accents, the iconic and comfortable hydropneumatic ride, and an ultra-quiet electric powertrain, seeking to use the design study to “bridge the gap between classic French avant-garde heritage and the future of sustainable mobility.” All in all, it’s now a bad attempt: the silhouette is instantly recognizable due to the four-door fastback profile, the LED headlights have the same form as the ones on the original but with modern light elements, there are slim exterior mirror cameras, and the triangle-shaped taillights also get modern LED touches. The nods to the past continue with the semi-covered rear wheels and the form of the doors. Inside, the concept is pretty simple: there’s blue leather everywhere with chrome trim and white piping; the iconic one-arm steering wheel makes a comeback despite having an integrated airbag, and the dashboard recalls the GS and GSA but with modern digital instrumentation. So, what do you think – yay or nay? Aurel has aimed high all his life (literally, at 16 he was flying gliders all by himself) so in 2006 he switched careers and got hired as a writer at his favorite magazine. Since then, his work has been published both by print and online outlets, most recently right here, on autoevolution.

title: Giselle Silva at '23 Points' in Career, Vows Powerful Finish for GS Caltex - 조선일보
content: Cuban star, nearing career's end, aims to repeat championship success with new teammate Tanacha Suksot “If I were to compare my volleyball career to a 25-point set, I’d say I’m at around 23 points.” Giselle Silva (35, Cuba), who led GS Caltex to last season’s championship and won both the V-League Regular Season Women’s Division MVP and Championship MVP, did not deny that her volleyball career has entered its final stretch. However, she emphasized that reaching “23 points” does not mean she will ease up as she approaches the end. Instead, she wants to pour all her strength and energy into securing the final points. “A professional athlete’s job is physical. If the time comes when I can no longer show the same power as before and must sit on the bench, I’ll step down. I want to finish my career while still demonstrating the same energy and power I have now. I must keep showing my relentless drive for victory until the end.” Silva is currently training in Hitachinaka City, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan. When she met with reporters at the Astemo Rivale training facility for the Japanese women’s volleyball team on September 11, she expressed pride at being the first foreign player in the V-League to spend four seasons with a single team. For Silva, who has traveled across the world playing volleyball, GS Caltex is a special team. She never expected to stay this long when she first arrived in Korea. Like before, she could have moved to a new country after one season for another challenge. But after one season in Korea, her perspective changed. Rather than packing her bags again and starting from scratch in an unfamiliar country, she wanted to stay where both she and her family felt comfortable. Seeing her daughter Ciana (6) adapt well and enjoy life in Korea deepened her desire to remain. Last season, Silva displayed monstrous power by recording a success rate of over 50% (50.63%) after 200 attack attempts in the postseason, leading GS Caltex to a perfect 6-0 championship run. Despite chronic knee pain, she scored over 30 points in six consecutive games, delivering a valuable trophy to the team. However, she insisted the championship was not her individual achievement. “There were ups and downs, but we found solutions. I’m proud of my teammates who worked with me to overcome difficulties and achieve victory. They supported me a lot.” Her faith in the team remains unchanged ahead of the new season. When asked what gives her confidence in reclaiming the top spot, Silva did not hesitate. “It’s confidence. We did it last season. Why can’t we do it again this season? If every player on the court shares that confidence, I believe we can repeat the feat. Most importantly, my teammates have grown significantly. It’s visible.” This season, Silva has a formidable new teammate: Tanacha Suksot (26, Thailand), who faced her on the opposite side of the net in last season’s championship finals. Suksot, an outside hitter for the Thai national team who played for Korea Road Public Corporation last season, joined GS Caltex as an Asian Quota player this season. Silva recalled the intense rivalry with Suksot during the championship finals, where they exchanged fierce glances. When she first heard that her former opponent would become a teammate, Silva thought, “This will be fun.” “Tanacha is great at defense and has a fierce attack. Our chemistry will be good, and we’ll show fans exciting volleyball they’ll love.” Suksot also alleviates the offensive burden on Silva. When opponents focus on defending Silva, Suksot can open alternative attacking avenues, diversifying GS Caltex’s offense. The number most associated with Silva is “1,000.” She became the first V-League player to score over 1,000 points in three consecutive seasons. While it’s a remarkable record, it also reflects how heavily GS Caltex relied on her offense. “1,000 points? I don’t think it’s a perfect situation for the team if I’m the one scoring them. Still, this record holds personal pride. It’s a number built by enduring an entire season with strong physical and mental resilience.” GS Caltex head coach Lee Young-taek said, “It’s true Silva handles many attacks, but her efficiency is close to 50%, which is high. Maximizing high-probability attacks is the path to victory.” Another pillar supporting Silva’s career is her family. Balancing motherhood and her athletic career while moving across the globe is not easy. Her husband, Luis, made it possible. “My husband’s life changed 180 degrees. He prioritized my career over his own to let me continue playing. Without his sacrifice and support, I wouldn’t have lasted this long. I can focus entirely on volleyball on the court because of him.” Asked how she wants to be remembered by V-League fans, Silva answered without hesitation: “I want to be remembered as a player who never gave up and kept fighting until the end.”

title: Tanacha Suksot Joins GS Caltex for Growth - 조선일보
content: Aiming to support Silva, embrace leadership, chase championship at new club [OSEN=Son Chan-ik Reporter] “I thought I needed to throw myself into a new environment to develop further.” Choosing change over familiarity, Tanacha Suksot (26), an outside hitter from the Thai national team, embarks on a new challenge wearing the GS Caltex uniform. Tanacha, who took her first steps in the V-League in 2023 with Korea Expressway Corporation, described her time there as “one of the best memories of my life.” Though filled with good memories, she did not want to become complacent. She judged that changing her environment was necessary to grow as a volleyball player. Meeting Tanacha at GS Caltex’s training camp in Japan on the 12th, she stated, “I felt that a change in environment was necessary to develop further as a volleyball player. Throwing myself into unfamiliar situations could be an opportunity to take another step forward in life.” The first club to reach out to Tanacha, who had decided to pursue change, was GS Caltex. She explained her decision to transfer, saying, “When I started considering a transfer, GS Caltex contacted me first. I wanted to join a team that highly valued my abilities.” Coincidentally, the team she faced in last season’s Championship Finals. From the opponent’s court, GS Caltex was a team that was difficult to stop once they gained momentum. Reflecting on it, Tanacha said, “Once they gained momentum, it was really hard to break their flow. The ‘chemistry’ between the players seemed very tight. I could feel their trust in each other even on the court.” Now, she has directly entered that tight-knit environment. There are differences too. Her position within the team has changed. Born in 2000, Tanacha was relatively young at Korea Expressway Corporation, where there were many veterans. At GS Caltex, she has become someone who must lead the younger players. She laughed, saying, “At Korea Expressway Corporation, when we divided into senior and junior teams during training, I was the oldest in the junior team. But here, I’m on the senior side to the point where I can’t show any immaturity.” One of the aspects GS Caltex expects from Tanacha is balance in attack. Until last season, the team’s offense was heavily concentrated on Gisele Silva, who boasts formidable attacking power, having become the first in V-League history to surpass 1,000 points for three consecutive seasons. There are expectations that Tanacha’s addition will reduce Silva’s offensive burden. However, Tanacha shook her head at the expression “I need to lessen Silva’s burden.” “Volleyball is a team sport. When all players participate in the attack, it becomes easier and more fun. Rather than thinking, ‘I need to reduce Silva’s burden,’ I believe it’s important for each player to fulfill their role.” Silva also welcomed the new teammate. After hearing that Tanacha would join GS Caltex, she expressed anticipation, saying, “She’s a player who works hard on defense and has good attacking skills. I think we can play fun volleyball together.” Hearing Silva’s words, Tanacha smiled brightly. “I’m really grateful for those words. It’s very meaningful to me. Becoming a better player together—that’s the image of a volleyball player I aspire to.” The values Tanacha pursues are clear. She considers being remembered as a “good teammate” as important as individual achievements. She said, “I can’t always play well. There are days when things go well and days when my performance doesn’t meet expectations. But being a good teammate is something I can strive for. When I look back on my volleyball career, I hope to be remembered as ‘a good teammate.’” That’s why she believes her role becomes more important when the game doesn’t go as planned. She approaches her teammates first, saying, “It’s okay. Let’s try again,” to lift the atmosphere. This mindset also reflects the unique culture of Thai volleyball. The characteristic of Thai volleyball that Tanacha highlighted is “volleyball that is enjoyed.” She explained, “Even if Thai players make mistakes, they don’t dwell on them too deeply. They smile and quickly move on to the next play. I think this mindset keeps the atmosphere alive and improves performance.” Overcoming physical disadvantages with diverse attacks is also a strength of Thai volleyball. “Since Thai players aren’t generally tall, we use a lot of combinations. Instead of attacking from just one spot, we move inside and outside to add variety to our attacks. I want to showcase this a lot this season.” Off the court, she is also active in building a “good team.” Her love for board games is not just a hobby but a way to get closer to her teammates. Tanacha explained, “If everyone just looks at their phones during free time, there’s no opportunity to talk while facing each other. Playing board games naturally makes us sit across from each other, share stories, and get to know each other better. I believe the closeness and trust built off the court eventually show on the court.” Wearing a new uniform and standing at a new starting line, Tanacha’s goal is clear: winning the championship. Although she experienced the joy of finishing first in the regular league with Korea Expressway Corporation, she did not reach the top of the Championship Finals. She emphasized, “I want to win the championship while doing my best. I will never give up on that goal.” Even in the process of chasing her goal, she doesn’t want to lose her own color. A player who chases the ball until the end and, when the team falters, is the first to smile and reach out to her teammates—that is the image Tanacha is drawing at GS Caltex. “I want to always be a teammate who gives good energy. This season, I’ll smile a lot.” /what@osen.co.kr

title: Candidate aghast at $500Gs bill for 'field with fence' dog park - torontosun.com
content: A candidate for council says he was told that spending half a million dollars to fence in a dog park is 'just the way it is' at Toronto City Hall See more Toronto Sun on Google — save as a Preferred Source How do you spend half a million dollars fencing in a field? Shawn Allen thinks City Hall has a spending problem, and his first, best example is the new off-leash dog park at Lawrence Ave. E and Starspray Blvd. – east of Port Union Rd.  He wants to be the next city councillor for Scarborough-Rouge Park, and for him the project has been something of a crash course in Toronto politics. “It’s a field with a fence. We’re paying for a fence. That’s what it is,” Allen told the Toronto Sun. “We’re paying to fence in a space – I think it’s 800 square metres, if I’m not mistaken – and we’re paying half a million dollars for that. And the majority of the cost is consulting fees, mobilization fees, arborists, geotechnical engineers, all these things. “Why do we need a geotechnical engineer to put a fence around grass? The dogs were running along the grass perfectly fine before they put up the dog park. Why can’t the dogs run along the grass and just fence it in?” Subscribe now to read the latest news in your city and across Canada. City Hall hasn’t provided an answer for the “why.” While the park was designed with input from residents in Scarborough-Rouge Park ward, the plan never went before committee to be scrutinized by city councillors and the public. The city wouldn’t confirm the project’s $500,000 price when asked by the Sun. The only official number comes from a motion by the incumbent councillor, Neethan Shan, to redirect $200,000 in funding for improvements from a nearby park, the Royal Rouge Tot Lot, to the off-leash area. Allen said he’s confident in the price because of a conversation with the project coordinator. “I said, why does it cost 500,000? She’s like, ha ha, that’s just the way it is. I go, what do you mean that’s just the way it is, ha-ha-ha? “We gotta figure this out. This city’s going broke.” In a statement, City Hall said construction at both the dog park and the Royal Rouge Tot Lot should be complete this fall. A final project cost and name for the dog park are still to come. Your noon-hour look at what's happening in Toronto and beyond. Please try again The city did not address questions about what the redirection of funds means for the Tot Lot, Allen’s conversation with the planning official or why a dog park would need a six-figure budget. Allen said he’s a dog owner and is in favour of off-leash parks – “but I’m just looking at the cost.” “For 500,000, you could house 108 people at $2,200 a month, so what’s the priority?” Shan redirected the Tot Lot funds with a member’s motion during May’s City Council meeting. While councillors can debate such motions, they typically draw little attention and this one passed with a quick show of hands. In an emailed statement, Shan focused less on the off-leash park and more on the Tot Lot improvements, which had a $300,000 budget – but got $530,000 in funding. Shan said he secured money from a playground enhancement program to pay for more amenities, including an accessible picnic table, a fitness pod and more play features. That funding allowed him to send the $200,000, from a pool of what’s known as Section 37 money, to the dog park budget. (While the Sun asked why a dog park would need a half-million-dollar budget, Shan did not address this in his statement.) “The kids didn’t get less money, they got more,” Shan wrote. “We listened to the community, improved the original plan and secured more investment to deliver more for residents.” Shan’s a rookie councillor but a veteran politician. He spent years as a school board trustee in both York Region and Toronto, then briefly served as city councillor for Scarborough-Rouge River, winning a 2017 byelection in what was Ward 42 in the city’s former 44-ward model. The ward map was redrawn, and he narrowly lost to Jennifer McKelvie in 2018’s election. When McKelvie left last year for Parliament, Shan won another byelection, while Allen placed third. The left-wing advocacy group Progress Toronto – founded by Mayor Olivia Chow’s political lieutenant Michal Hay – endorsed Shan last year, hailing him as a “progressive champion.” But Allen said constituents tell him that Shan is hard to get ahold of. He said City Hall is failing to provide Toronto with “value of service.” “The city is a corporation,” Allen said. “We have all these school board trustees as executives on the board of something that they’re not familiar with.” Allen was born and raised in Scarborough, and has run a mortgage brokerage for about two decades. Times are tight for many Torontonians, and Allen thinks City Hall isn’t helping. “We have food bank lines wrapped around the corner in West Hill. People are hungry,” he said. “People have mortgage arrears, people have tax arrears and the mayor’s committed to raising property taxes next year at the rate of inflation. Well, we’re still catching up from the 20% you raised it over the past three years, so now you’re going to put people behind the 8-ball even more … We can’t ask homeowners to find savings when the city’s not doing the same.” Postmedia is committed to maintaining a lively but civil forum for discussion. title: BMW F 450 GS Price Hike: Check New Variant-Wise Prices - Motoroids
content: Months after launching the much-awaited F 450 GS, BMW Motorrad has revised the prices of the ADV in India. Introduced as the brand’s new entry point into the GS family, buyers will now have to spend up to ₹30,000 more depending on the variant. The price hike applies across all three versions, with no new features or mechanical updates included in this revision. The F 450 GS is manufactured in India through BMW Motorrad’s partnership with TVS Motor Company. It replaced the G 310 GS as the brand’s smallest GS adventure motorcycle in the country. The Base and Exclusive versions have received a ₹25,000 price hike, while the top-spec GS Trophy gets the highest increase of ₹30,000. All prices listed below are ex-showroom. The GS Trophy continues as the most expensive version and comes with extra equipment, including BMW’s ERC (Easy Ride Clutch) system. This technology reduces the need to operate the clutch manually during gear shifts. Each variant is offered with a single colour option. The Base and Exclusive variants come in Cosmic Black, while the GS Trophy features Racing Blue with red and white graphics. BMW has left the engine completely unchanged. The F 450 GS continues to be powered by a 420cc, liquid-cooled, parallel-twin engine that produces 47bhp and 43Nm of torque. It is paired with a six-speed gearbox and features a slipper clutch. The use of a twin-cylinder engine separates the F 450 GS from the older G 310 GS, which relied on a single-cylinder motor. The F 450 GS is built on a tubular steel frame. It features a 43mm KYB upside-down front fork and a KYB rear monoshock, offering 180mm of suspension travel at both ends. The motorcycle rides on a 19-inch front wheel and a 17-inch rear wheel with dual-purpose tyres. The motorcycle has a seat height of 845mm. It provides an upright riding position and built-in wind protection for riders planning longer journeys. A 6.5-inch TFT display comes standard, supporting smartphone connectivity and navigation functions. Road, Rain and Enduro riding modes are offered as standard. The higher variants add Enduro Pro mode and extra electronic equipment. Other features include heated grips and adjustable levers. While the GS Trophy benefits from the ERC system, cruise control is not offered on any variant. The BMW F 450 GS now starts at Rs 4.95 lakh and goes up to Rs 5.60 lakh. Nothing else has been added with the latest price revision, so the higher prices are the only change for buyers.

title: "My volleyball is 23 points; full power goes to deuce." GS's Silva, who never stops, declares a 'full swing' until the very end - starnewskorea.com
content:
Foreign player Gisele Silva (35), currently undergoing training camp in Hitachinaka City, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan, has expressed her determination for the upcoming season. According to a press release from GS Caltex on the 12th, Silva, who led GS Caltex to a championship last season and swept both the regular league and championship finals MVP awards, compared her career to '23 points' out of a perfect 25-point volleyball set. She said, "If I cannot show the same power as before and have to stay on the bench, I should step aside, but until the moment I score the final point, I want to pour out my current energy and power." Silva has become the first foreign player in V-League history to spend four consecutive seasons with a single club, revealing her deep affection for life in Korea and the team. Last season, despite chronic knee pain during the playoffs, she recorded an attack success rate of 50.63% and led the team to a perfect 6-0 championship run. Silva credited her teammates for the victory and expressed strong confidence in winning again this season. The synergy with Tanatcha Soksot, who joined as a new Asia quota player this season, is also a key expectation. Regarding Tanatcha, whom she faced last season in the championship finals, Silva stated, "She is a player with sharp defense and attack, so we should be able to show great chemistry together." Tanatcha's addition is seen as a tactical card that will help disperse the opponent's focused attention and offensive burden on Silva. On the record of being the first in V-League history to surpass 1,000 points in three consecutive seasons, Silva explained, "While high reliance on attacks from specific players is not an ideal situation for the team as a whole, it is a proud record reflecting my strong physique and mental resilience that allowed me to endure a full season." GS Caltex head coach Lee Young-taek also highlighted Silva's impressive attack success rate nearing 50%, emphasizing the importance of high-probability attacks. Finally, Silva expressed gratitude to her husband for his dedication in balancing her athletic career with parenting and told fans, "I want to remain a player who never gave up and fought until the very end." <© STARNEWS. title: Thanacha Suksom Stresses Teamwork in New GS Caltex Role - 조선일보
content: Thai Star Balances Offense, Fosters Camaraderie After Transfer from Korea Expressway “I thought that to develop further, I needed to throw myself into a new environment.” Thanacha Suksom, 26 years old, an outside hitter from the Thai national team, chose a new challenge this season. After joining the Korea Expressway Corporation in 2023 and competing in the V-League, he described his time with the team as “one of the best memories of my life.” Still, he opted for change. Rather than staying in a familiar environment, he wanted to test himself in a new one. Meeting Thanacha at GS Caltex’s Japanese training camp on September 12, he said, “I felt that a change of environment was necessary to take my volleyball career to the next level. Throwing myself into unfamiliar situations could be an opportunity to move forward in life.” The first team to reach out was GS Caltex. “When I started considering a transfer, GS Caltex contacted me first,” he said. “I wanted to join a team that highly valued me.” Coincidentally, GS Caltex was the team he faced in last season’s championship finals. At the time, observing them from the opposing court, he found them a tough opponent with few weaknesses. “Once they gained momentum, it was really hard to break their flow. The ‘chemistry’ between the players seemed incredibly tight. I could feel their trust in each other even on the court.” The biggest change Thanacha feels now is being part of the “senior line.” Born in 2000, he was relatively young at Korea Expressway Corporation, where veterans were abundant. But at GS Caltex, he has become a leader responsible for guiding younger teammates. “At Korea Expressway, I was the oldest in the ‘younger group’ during training, but here, I’m firmly on the senior side—no room to act young,” he laughed. One role GS Caltex expects of Thanacha is balancing the team’s offense. He needs to share the burden that previously fell heavily on Gisele Silva, who led the team’s attacks last season. Silva became the first player in V-League history to score over 1,000 points in three consecutive seasons. However, Thanacha shook his head at the idea of “easing Silva’s burden.” “Volleyball is a team sport. When everyone participates in attacks, it becomes easier and more fun. Rather than ‘I must reduce Silva’s load,’ each player fulfilling their role is key.” Silva also welcomes the new teammate. Upon hearing of Thanacha’s joining, she said, “She works hard on defense and has good attacking skills. I think we can play fun volleyball together.” When relayed Silva’s words, Thanacha smiled and said, “I’m really grateful for those words. It means a lot to me. Becoming a better player together is exactly what I want as a volleyball athlete.” “You can’t always perform well in volleyball. There are days when things go smoothly and days when your skills don’t show. But being a good teammate is something I can strive for. When I look back on my volleyball career, I hope to be remembered as ‘a good teammate.’” That’s why Thanacha’s role becomes clearer when matches don’t go as planned. He is the first to approach a teammate and say, “It’s okay. Let’s try again.” This mindset also reflects Thai volleyball culture. Thanacha highlighted its biggest feature as “enjoying the game.” “Thai players don’t dwell too long on mistakes. They laugh and quickly move on to the next play. I believe this attitude keeps the atmosphere alive and improves performance.” Overcoming physical disadvantages with diverse attacks is another characteristic of Thai volleyball. “Since Thai players aren’t generally tall, we use a lot of combinations,” he said. “Instead of attacking from one spot, we move inside and outside to add variety. I want to showcase this style a lot this season.” Off the court, Thanacha also focuses on building a “good team.” His love for board games isn’t just a hobby—it’s a form of “teamwork training” to bond with teammates. “If everyone just stares at their phones during free time, there’s no chance to talk face-to-face. Board games make us sit together naturally, leading to conversations and deeper understanding. The closeness and trust built off the court eventually show on it,” he explained. Thanacha’s goal this season, in his new uniform, is obviously a championship. With Korea Expressway, he experienced the joy of finishing first in the regular league but didn’t reach the championship finals’ summit. “I want to do my best and win the championship. I won’t give up on that goal,” he said. Even in the pursuit of the title, he doesn’t want to lose his unique color. On the court, he chases the ball until the end, and when the team falters, he’s the first to smile and reach out to a teammate—this is how he envisions himself. “I want to be a teammate who always gives good energy. This season, I’ll smile a lot.”

title: What a Fed Rate Hike Could Mean for US Stocks - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Investors are pricing in a higher likelihood that the Federal Reserve will hike rates after core CPI inflation rose in August more than economists had estimated. However, a rate hike may not keep the US stock market from climbing higher, says Jonathan Shugar, head of Cross Asset Sales in Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities, on The Markets podcast. Companies reported strong earnings growth in the second quarter, and valuations near the 10-year average are not stretched, he explains. Shugar also discusses why a Fed hike may not restrain investment in artificial intelligence, the risks in longer-term interest rates, and the potential opportunity for investors in consumer experience stocks. Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Friday, September 11th. Before we start, I want to acknowledge that it's 25 years since the 9/11 attacks. As our chairman and CEO, David Solomon, said in remarks, "Our firm joins the community in honoring the lives lost that day, as well as the first responders, recovery workers, and survivors, and everyone who suffered from 9/11 related illnesses." I'm also joined today on the Goldman Sachs trading floor by John Shugar. John is head of cross-asset sales within FICC and Equities. John, thanks so much for joining us on The Markets. Jonathan Shugar: Thank you for having me, Chris. Great to be here. Chris Hussey: Well, first time, long time for you, I know. Tell us a little bit about cross-asset sales. That could encompass anything. What exactly is it? Jonathan Shugar: What we like to do is be like our clients, which is ultra-flexible as to where the opportunity set is. That's really what drives it. The team is about 25 people, specialists across equities, derivatives, execution, credit, rates, and FX. And so really what we're able to help people do is capture these inflection points in markets, whether that's going from a growth equity cycle to a credit cycle, or whether that is looking at asymmetric hedges. And you've seen the utility of that ever since the subprime crisis to different rate hiking cycles or credit protection, where we look for asymmetric hedges. And we'll talk a little bit more about that later on. Chris Hussey: Yeah. Well, it sounds like having the inflection guy here is perfect because we just got the CPI report. The FOMC meets next week. Looks like we might be in for an inflection. What do you make of the CPI report and the reaction that the market's had so far? Jonathan Shugar: So, I think that the market reaction is telling you that they're going to hike next week. We have something like 84% odds priced for that, and for 50 bps before year-end. That's not to say that inflation has not followed some of what the people who want to hold say, which is you haven't seen shelter inflation continue to go and goods inflation moderated. It was really driven by things like communication services. That being said, with it being so hot and the Fed having said they're data-dependent, the market is telling them that in some ways it's actually more dangerous not to hike because you might lose control of the back end in that case, and that's one of the bigger risks to the market. Chris Hussey: Yeah, it's a great point, cause the Fed controls the front end through their Fed funds rate, but the back end is controlled by the markets, and the markets can do anything they want there. Let's talk a little bit about equities for a second here, because this also is back to school week, and we've had a series of things that always happens in the back to school, and people come back and they're trading heavily. The market, though, has kind of flat-lined since early August. What do you make of the rally that we've had and where do you see it going from here? Jonathan Shugar: So we've had some near-term challenges. Momentum has had an extraordinarily tough last two months. When you look at technical levels here, you have both CTA and systematic flows against you in the near term. That being said, we just finished our Communacopia conference. One of the biggest themes in the market right now is AI. The companies coming out of there could not have been more bullish. And to the people who say the market is expensive, we're trading at a 19 PE. That's the 10-year average. We've had S&P earnings growth of something like 30% on the second quarter. So, if you look at that, you basically have a market where all of the heavy lifting has actually been done on the earnings side. And when you think about the drivers going forward, there's terrific opportunities within various AI consumer sectors which are off highs, to really say that, well, over the next few weeks we may have a lot more speed bumps. But if you and I are sitting here at year-end or we're sitting here next year, we're talking about an S&P that's probably well over 8,000. Chris Hussey: Okay, John, let's examine de-globalization because your customers can invest anywhere in anything all at once, and there have been a lot of geopolitical risks. We're seeing it in the oil tape. What are your customers saying about those geopolitical risks today? Jonathan Shugar: So, one of the most interesting things has been the things that really impacted the market negatively when you think about Liberation Day as the original tariff announcement. Those have become less relevant to price action as we go forward, and it's a trend that we've really seen since COVID, which is the duration of opportunity to take advantage of dislocations to the market is getting less and less, and the moves to correct to the upside are much more violent. Now, when you think about geopolitical risk out there, there's certainly things which are near term. You mentioned oil. If you look at Brent right now, you're trading around 104, but you look out one year, you're buying Brent at, with a seven handle on it. So, this is still viewed as a more near-term problem. That doesn't mean you can't have local disruptions. On the product side, whether it's gasoline, diesel, heating oil, probably looks incrementally worse for Europe than the US, but that can certainly be something that comes up. All of that should be relatively short duration in terms of impact but can certainly drive local price action. When we think more broadly, there are geopolitical impacts on both the positive and negative side. Obviously there's a good reason why you might want to look at a country like Brazil, and we've seen investors increasingly look to buy upside there as they're going into an election in October. Chris Hussey: Brazil. When the market zigs, you zag. I love it. Okay. You're a risk guy. Let's talk a little bit more broadly about risks here because I know you have a view. What are the risks out there that you're watching and how do you wanna hedge them? Jonathan Shugar: So, as we think about what the largest risk on the board is, it really, outside of some of the true tells, which are global geopolitical risk exploding is really in the back end of the rate curve. And that is because, one, there's natural impulse for this to be higher. You have global fiscal deficits. This is not just a US problem. This is everywhere. You have a ton of AI issuance, so hyperscalers doing about $800 billion of CapEx this year. Our analysts estimate something around $1.2 trillion next year. So, there's a lot of natural supply which is competing for money. Now, if you get a really sharp move in rates, cause equities can tolerate higher rates. It's really just the pace of change that has the biggest impact. So, the way we like to hedge that is really in two ways: either buying outright payers or payer spreads on the back end, the 30-year part of the swap curve, or looking out and doing something like a CMS cap, which is the shape of the curve between front and back end, and we think that there's good returns out there. Now, we always love 10 X-type trades. On reasonable strikes, you can probably still make five to six X your premium. And so that's what we're talking to investors about now. Chris Hussey: Five to six X. I thought everything was 10X, but okay. You say equities can tolerate higher rates, but do they tolerate higher rates because as long as the rates are going higher because of inflation, equities are indexed to inflation, so they're a nominal asset, so they go up? What happens if the higher rates are tied to something more like a debasement trade? Jonathan Shugar: So, if they're tied to a true tail risk debasement trade, that would obviously be negative in the short term for equities. If you get true hyperinflation, and you can go back to Zimbabwe or anything you want, that could be really good for equities because they are a nominal asset. That being said, I think the reason people are thinking about all of this is, one, economic growth remains good. The fact is that hiking25 or 50 basis points doesn't change the need for the strongest balance sheet companies in the world to be investing heavily in CapEx, given how transformative a technology AI is going to be, and the consumer outside of the low end still is okay. And so, you compare that to the fact that most consumer stocks are trading 30% plus off their 52-week highs. There just seems a real disconnect here. And so, as you think about equities going forward, people got very surprised by things like biotech performing so well. And biotech, another thing that typically has a lot of correlation negatively to higher end rates being higher. Well, I think consumer and there are pockets of that we like, there are pockets of that we don't like, could be the thing that surprises into your end. By the way, another plug for our conferences, we've got our consumer conference next week. So, we're going to know a lot more after that. Chris Hussey: Okay, you gave us a great hedge trade, but give us one more. What's the trade? Jonathan Shugar: So, I think that there's a lot that can be done here. Number one, within consumer, there's both longs and things that we're more cautious on. On the long side, the experiential type names, whether it's cruise, whether it's events, things that people really want to do and spend money on, especially at the high end, that continues to see a lot of growth. On the flip side, there have been companies releasing agents for consumers. Well, guess what? If you don't have to spend two hours to switch your phone plan to a cheaper plan that's probably something that could be really impactful, and so we're a little bit more cautious on some of the impacts there. We mentioned AI briefly. A lot of the CapEx picks and shovels are trading well below market multiples. A lot of the semis type names trading well below market multiples. You're seeing capital return in some of those places and other interesting things. We think this is a temporary air pocket and those have good runway ahead of them. Chris Hussey: Terrific. Sum us up for this here. What are you watching for next week and the weeks ahead that we should be keeping our eyes on? Jonathan Shugar: So clearly watching the Fed next week, I think that's something where the press conference is going to be a lot more impactful than the actual if they do hike, hike. If they don't hike, that's actually very interesting and may have impact of its own. Outside of that, I think that any clarification on kind of the big picture questions from corporates as you go through the rest of the year on the efficacy of AI in terms of increasing revenue will get people really, really excited again. Outside of that, watching the Giants on Sunday. Hoping that's not another tough season to be a Giants fan. Chris Hussey: J-E-T-S, Jets, Jets, Jets. John Shugar, you're a wealth of information. Thanks so much for joining us. Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening. title: “One of the Biggest Statements So Far”: Skatta on Karol G’s “BbY WOW” Global Success - Kaboom Magazine
content: Our latest digital magazine is available for download - CLICK HERE >> “BbY WOW,” which samples the iconic “Coolie Dance Riddim,” gives the classic beat another major global moment. “This beat was different,” Burrell reflects on its enduring impact For years, music producer and industry figure Skatta Burrell has continued to reap the success of his iconic juggling, the Coolie Dance Riddim, as the 2003 production continues to find new life across international music. The compilation, listed by Rolling Stone among the 25 Riddims That Shaped Jamaican Music, became one of dancehall’s biggest international crossovers, powering hits including Elephant Man’s “Jook Gal,” Mr. Vegas’ “Pull Up,” Bounty Killer’s “Yuh Gwan” and more. Its reach stretched even further through Pitbull’s Latin smash “Culo” and Nina Sky’s Billboard Hot 100 Top 10 hit “Move Ya Body,” which was later remixed featuring Vybz Kartel. “The experience of witnessing multiple samples and remixes of the Coolie Dance Riddim is something I’ve been witnessing almost yearly since its release in 2003,” Burrell said, reflecting on the riddim’s longevity. More than two decades later, Coolie Dance continues to move beyond dancehall floors and into the global mainstream. Beyoncé moved to its pulse during her 2023 Renaissance World Tour, while Kehlani sampled the riddim on her 2024 viral hit “After Hours.” Its latest major moment comes through Colombian superstar Karol G, alongside Spanish artistes Judeline and rusowsky, whose “BbY WOW” samples the riddim and climbed to No. 1 on both the Billboard Global 200 and Billboard Global Excl. U.S. charts. The song generated 42.3 million global streams from August 28 to September 3 and has surpassed 116 million streams on Spotify. “This ‘BbY WOW’ hit is by far one of the biggest statements so far, and especially being a Spanish-language song, it seems to be captivating the world due to its infectious melodies and the dynamics and groove from the Coolie Dance beat,” Burrell shared. “No words can explain the gratitude and reassurance I get just knowing I created music that is definitely timeless.” Latin superstar Karol G gives the classic beat another major global moment. For Burrell, the riddim’s continued global success also validates the creative instincts behind a beat that sounded different from much of what surrounded it at the time. “I’ve always known this beat was different and out of the norm, and it reminds me that trying to fit in is never the way to achieving greatness,” he said. “What matters most is the way music makes you feel, and its main purpose is to evoke emotions and movement.” While Burrell admits he never predicted just how far Coolie Dance would travel, he always believed there was more to come from the production. “This global impact was never forecasted. However, I’ve always had that confident assurance inside that there’s always more to come from this Coolie Dance Riddim,” he added. title: GS Shop Bets on Lace Trend to Drive Fall Fashion Sales - Seoul Economic Daily
content: Jason Wu Lace Camisoles Draw 120 Million Won in Orders Clothing with lace detailing is drawing attention as "lacecore" emerges as a fall fashion trend. Lacecore applies elements borrowed from lingerie — lace and satin fabrics and slip dresses — to everyday wear. Rather than putting lace front and center, the recent approach layers it under knitwear or jackets as an accent. Fall-winter fashion items with lace detailing are winning strong consumer response at GS Shop, industry sources said on the 12th. Two lace camisole styles, first introduced on the 29th of last month during a broadcast launching Jason Wu's fall-winter line, drew orders for about 2,000 units worth 120 million won. The pieces pair lace trim with softly lustrous satin and feature a diagonal hem, making them easy to layer under jackets or knitwear. La Piaf's new fall-winter "lace detail knit top" also sold more than 1,000 units during a broadcast on the 11th. Morgan's "lace satin skirt," which adds lace at the hem, drew orders for about 2,000 units in its first broadcast. GS Shop plans to air the skirt again on the 12th. Along with responding to the lacecore trend, GS Shop is expanding layering pieces aimed at unpredictable autumn weather, adding garments that can be worn in combination depending on the temperature. Late last month, the company held a "26 FW Fashion Showcase," unveiling a large lineup of fall arrivals from its exclusive fashion brands through its TV home shopping channel and mobile app. For this season, it expanded transitional-weather items such as shirts, blouses, lightweight long-sleeve T-shirts and cardigans, while strengthening pieces that layer well with other garments, including vests and bustiers. The focus was on versatility — items that can be worn alone in early fall and paired with jackets and other outerwear as temperatures drop. One example is La Piaf's "open-up vest and cardigan layered set," which can be styled three ways: the vest alone, the cardigan alone, or the two together. Worn together, the design lets the vest's hem show naturally below the cropped cardigan. Following the ruffled blouses that proved popular last spring and summer, the brand also introduced a "pin-tuck volume blouse" with three-quarter sleeves and pleated detailing. Jason Wu released a fall version of its "Vera Essential Jacket," a summer hit, adding UV protection and quick-drying functions. Core Authentic reinforced its outerwear lines that drew strong customer response last season, broadening its selection with items including the "cupra stadium bomber," noted for its light weight and subtle sheen, along with a hooded field jacket and a high-neck faux-leather blouson. "Order value for our exclusive fashion brands grew about 15.6% year-on-year in the first half, leading growth across the entire fashion category and contributing to earnings improvement," a GS Shop official said. "We have prepared products that can be worn in a variety of ways from the transitional season through winter, so customers don't lose out on newness and style even in unpredictable weather." title: Taylor Townsend, Katerina Siniakova win US Open women's doubles - ESPN
content: NEW YORK -- Taylor Townsend was tight, wasn't moving well and could sense she was swinging her racket early in the US Open women's doubles final. "I wanted this really badly, and I knew that I wanted it," she said. "I felt it in my body and my spirit because I was so nervous." Playing partner Katerina Siniakova talked her through the rough start Friday, and then they found their groove and rolled. Townsend and Siniakova completed their career Grand Slam as a team by defeating the wild-card pair of Ashlyn Krueger and Robin Montgomery for their first US Open doubles title together. "It just means the world to me," Townsend said. "This really means everything to me, not only just to be able to win the US Open but to be able to complete a career Slam." It looked dicey early, when Townsend and Siniakova lost the first three games and dropped the first set. At one point, the ball dropped between them, an uncharacteristic mistake for the top two women's doubles players on the planet. Then the top seeds started looking like it with aggressive shots at the net, and they took control of the match on the way to a 5-7, 6-0, 6-2 victory at Arthur Ashe Stadium. "The match was very tight, very tough for us, but we found a way to win it," Siniakova said. "We found a solution. I'm just really happy that we have this one and we can celebrate it together." The result validated Townsend's confidence in her play after getting knocked out in singles by No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka. The 30-year-old American expressed confidence in her tennis at the time, knowing she still had another opportunity in doubles. That turned into her fourth major championship after she and Siniakova won Wimbledon in 2024, the Australian Open in 2025 and the French Open earlier this year. It was Siniakova's 12th Grand Slam title after winning seven with fellow Czech player Barbora Krejcikova and one with Coco Gauff. "It helps to have someone that's been here so many times and who has been able to get over the hump -- what is it, 12? Twelve times," Townsend said. It was an impressive run for Krueger and Montgomery, who respectively rank 570th and 610th in doubles and went through each half of defending champions Erin Routliffe and Gabriela Dabrowski separately in the quarterfinals and semifinals. Krueger and Montgomery reunited five years after winning the US Open girls' doubles title and advancing a round at the women's level in 2021. "We're both just trying to take it all in," Montgomery said. "What we've just done has been amazing. I think we did forget that we were offered a wild card, so I'm just glad we made good use of it." Townsend and Siniakova, who fell short against Routliffe and Dabrowski in the final a year ago, got a happier result this time. Townsend dropped to her knees after the final point and was all smiles as she said to Siniakova that they finally did it. "If flipping the script had a face," Townsend said, "you'd see my face." A year after famously sipping the tournament's signature cocktail, the Honey Deuce, at the news conference after losing in the women's doubles final, Townsend had one in each hand this time. Carrying just one, Siniakova asked Townsend, "Next year, you have three and I have two?" -- setting the table for the duo to already start thinking about a repeat.
